newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Kirch begins to lift veil of secrecy.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kirch begins to lift veil of secrecy.

text.p: Bavarian media tycoon Leo Kirch, one of German television industry's most guarded figures, is lifting the veil of secrecy that shrouds his media empire.

Kirch's seven managing directors yesterday began courting journalists in what they described as the first step of a new policy of openness aimed at improving what they see as a skewed picture of the man and his media enterprise.
The 70-year-old Kirch was not present, but Jan Mojto, the head of programme acquisitions, said, 'This is the start of something. We do not have anything to hide."
Kirch's particular brand of Glasnost is nothing short of a cultural revolution at the media group that has a vast arsenal of films and TV stations like SAT1 and DF1 digital pay TV.
Kirch has often drawn criticism from local media during its battles with arch rival Bertelsmann AG.

Bertelsmann enjoys a more positive image that stems from the liberal Protestant roots of Reinhard Mohn, who rebuilt the firm after World War Two from a minor bible publisher to become Europe's largest media conglomerate.
"The picture of Kirch that has been painted was of a lack of transparency, of something sinister in a way. A man in the background pulling strings," said Mojto, who has been with Kirch since 1980.
"The feeling we have is that the people who are writing about us do not understand what we are doing."
Kirch has ignored the sniping for decades. But recent events apparently convinced him the time had come to grant outsiders a closer look at his enterprise.

German media have heaped scorn on the Kirch's efforts to secure a bank loan with the assistance of a state development bank. Smelling political cronyism, media outrage forced the Bavarian government to back out of the deal.
A series of critical articles about Kirch and his finances in the German press followed and had an unexpected impact.
"This did not affect our dealings with business partners in industry, but I believe it did not have a positive impact on our dealings with the banks," Mojto explained.
Highlighting its new policy of openness, Kirch Group dismissed media reports of an impending financial collapse by issuing vague, but unprecedented statements about its earnings.

"The Kirch Group's earnings situation is stable and in the past years it has achieved double-digit returns on sales," it said in a statement. "The value of our financial assets alone are comfortably above current and future credit volumes."
The company said it achieved revenues of over a billion marks ($548.2 million) a year from film licences, but gave no details of overall group turnover.

Kirch and Bertelsmann appear to have finally buried the hatchet in their dispute over digital TV and are now awaiting European Commission approval of a deal that paves the way for the broad launch of digital TV later this year.
They will hold equal shares in Premiere, the German pay TV group with 1.5 million subscribers, and Premiere and Kirch's struggling DF1 digital pay TV firm will cooperate.

Anti-trust officials have expressed doubts about the deal if it involves a merger of Premiere and DF1, but Kirch Group officials assure this will not happen. Nevertheless, Premiere and DF1 will be partners not rivals.
"Independent of what the final structure is there will be no conflict of interest," said Dieter Hahn, in charge of sporting rights and spokesman for Kirch directors' committee.
Klaus Piette, Kirch director in charge of legal affairs, said the group had not yet registerd its plans with the European Commission but he expected approval this year.

Gottfried Zmeck, Kirch director in charge of DF1, said the digital broadcaster now has 50,000 subscribers. Once the deal with Premiere is approved, there will be a push to encourage Premiere's analogue customers to switch to digital TV.
"We think now that within the next 4-5 years there will be a total of three million digital TV subscribers in Germany," said Zmeck.
